en: The *Continued Brief Account of Eminent Monks of West Lake in Wulin*, the Main Collection, begins with the Jin dynasty and ends with the Song and Yuan dynasties; after that, no one continued it.

I have therefore supplemented it by including five masters from the end of the Yuan and the beginning of the Ming. Among them, Master Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben is traditionally said to reside at present-day Mount Wu.
In the Yunju Hermitage there still exist the hemp sandals worn by the Master.

However, upon examining his biography, memorial inscription, and correspondence with Guanglu, there is no mention whatsoever of his serving as abbot of Yunju. I have not dared to supplement the record to conform to worldly custom.
Furthermore, in the *Zhengji* (Correct Collection), the entire account of National Teacher Qian’s life is situated at Shuangjing; I have seen no record of him residing in the West [of Lin’an].
The actual record of Lake [Hu] seems to be deletable; it is provisionally retained here for further examination.

Regarding the five masters added [to the lineage], although one or two were born during the Yuan dynasty, their appearance in the world and parinirvāṇa occurred primarily during the Hongwu and Yongle reigns;
therefore, they are uniquely designated under the banner of "Our Dynasty" (the Ming). Future authors may continue this further. Recorded by the Cloud-Abode Śramaṇa Wu.
Recorded by Lin Zhuhong as a continuation and supplement to the catalog of various masters:
Chan Master Mingxing Yuanlang and Chan Master Chushi Xuyun Qi of the Great Ming.
*The Continued Brief Account of Eminent Monks of the West Lake in Wulin*,
compiled by Chan Master Long of Daming Konggu,
Chan Master Shan of Daming Dufeng, and Chan Master Mou of Daming Xueting.
Compiled by Yunqi Zhuhong of the Ming Dynasty.
The Chan Master Xingyuan Lang of the Great Ming:
His name was Huilang; his courtesy name was Xingyuan; his alternative style was Hanyi. He was born in the Yuan era in Huang... of Taizhou Prefecture.
Yan was born in the Xiangzhai residence; his mother was surnamed Chen. When he was seven years old, he suffered from carbuncles and nearly died.
He was placed upon a bed, and suddenly he vanished. After some time, he was found. When asked how this had happened, he said, "Recently while asleep, four youths carried me here;

there was nothing else to it. The next day, the carbuncles healed. Those who recognized him already knew that the Master had been protected by celestial deities. Having grown up, he could not bear [the worldly life].
While living among the laity, he went to rely upon Master Donggong at Baoguan Temple on Mount Lu in Yueqing, Yongjia, and there received the precepts.

Later, he traveled to Jingshan to visit Master Yuansou Duan. When Duan asked, "Does it come from the eastern ridge? Does it come from the western ridge? the Master pointed to his straw sandals and said: [They do.]
"This was bought for three copper coins. Duan said, "Not yet. Speak further. The Master said, "I am only like this;
I do not know how you, the Master, would act. Duan said, "Out of consideration that you have come from afar, I grant you thirty blows.
Thereupon, the Master realized its essential meaning. After a long time, he exhausted the depths of the treasury. Subsequently, he appeared in the world at Wufeng in Ningbo. [The] Ming Dynasty.
In the fifth year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Buddhist assembly on Mount Zhongshan.
The Master, along with the monk Letan Le, was summoned to participate. Subsequently, he resided at Lingyin for ten years; before long, however, he encountered an undeserved calamity.
He was arrested. Some urged the Master to plan for his own safety early on, but he paid no heed. With a serene expression, he went to the authorities;
before the interrogation had even begun, he recited a verse beneath the eaves of the hall and passed away while sitting upright.
The Great Illumination Master Chan Master Chushi Qi:
His name was Fan Qi, his style name was Chushi. He was a native of Xiangshan in Mingzhou and belonged to the Zhu clan. His mother was Lady Zhang.

On the day of Ding-si in the sixth month of the second year of the Yuanzhen era of the Yuan dynasty (the Bing-shen year), he was born while still in his swaddling clothes. A monk saw him and said to his father:
"This child will surely uphold the Buddha-dharma and illuminate this turbid age. At nine years of age, he received his formal training from Master Ne of Tianning Temple in Haiyan;
at sixteen, he became a monk; and at twenty, he attended upon his paternal great-uncle, Master Xun of Jinweng. While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he reached the passage:
"When seeing arises due to conditions, darkness becomes non-seeing; when non-clarity spontaneously manifests, then all appearances of darkness can never again obscure it."

At this point, there was an awakening; however, regarding the "one stroke" that transcends all, he still encountered an obstruction. When Yuan-sou Daowei, the Abbot of Mount Jing, took charge of the monastery, [Zhao] went to pay his respects and asked:
"What is it that 'the speech issues forth but is not sound, and the form stands before us but is not an object'? Yuan-sou immediately said:

When the Master spoke, it was not as sound; when he appeared before the Elder, he was not as an object. "Quick! Quick! the Master intended to offer a word in response, but the Elder let out a thunderous shout.
The Master was left stunned and withdrew. Subsequently, he was selected to participate in the transcription of the Tripitaka.

Upon arriving at Chongtian Gate in the capital, one night he heard the sound of drums atop a decorated pavilion and attained great enlightenment. He returned to the East and once again attended upon Yuansou.
The old man smiled and welcomed him, saying, "Be glad that the great matter is now concluded. Not long after, he took up residence at Fuzhen Temple in Haiyan.

In the *Yihai* year of the *Zhizhi* era (1335), he moved to Baoguo Temple in Hangzhou. On the eleventh day of the ninth month of the first year of the *Hongwu* era (1368), the Emperor summoned the Master to preach the Dharma at Jiangshan;
the Emperor was greatly pleased. In the seventh month of the following year, he was summoned once more on the twenty-sixth day.

The verse says: "The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, it is without arising or ceasing. A wooden horse neighs at night; the sun rises in the west. He passed away while sitting upright.

Upon cremation, his teeth, tongue, and rosary remained unharmed. There are twenty volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) and his *Xizhai Jingtushi* (Verses on the Pure Land from the Western Studio) circulating in the world."
Chan Master Long of the Great Ming’s Empty Valley (Kōnggǔ):
His name was Jǐnglóng; his courtesy name was Zǔtíng; his style name was Kōnggǔ. He was the son of the Chén family of Mount Yǒng on Dōngtíng in Gūsū.
His father was the layman Yuètán, and his mother was of the Jīn clan. He was born on the twelfth day of the seventh month in the Guiyou year of the Hongwu era. As a child...

At that time, he abstained from meat and sat in the lotus posture as if in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). In the *Renchen* year of the Yongle era, he received instruction in Chan meditation from Master Lan-yun of the White Lotus Society at Mount Bian.
Although he remained a layman, there were no eminent Chan masters from across the land—such as Master Gu-zhuo and others—with whom he did not seek an audience.
In the *Gengzi* year, he left the household life at Mount Huqiu; in the second year of the Xuande era, he went to Zhaokong Temple in Hangzhou to receive [ordination].
He observed the precepts and subsequently resided with his master at Lingyin for seven years. He then traveled to Mount Tianmu to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda, where he stayed for one year.

Through diligent and arduous investigation, he suddenly attained realization. He went to visit Lanyun to disclose his insight, and Lanyun certified his attainment. Lanyun was the twenty-fourth generation descendant of Linji.
The Master’s writings comprise thirty volumes of the *Konggu ji* (Empty Valley Collection), through which his mastery of the Heart-Mind School was thoroughly realized.

His intellectual discernment was sharp and outstanding; he was thoroughly versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism, and his understanding of phenomena and principle were seamlessly integrated. The Grand Minister of Rites, Lord Wu, composed an inscription for him.
When the Master was fifty-two years old, he himself composed a stupa inscription at Xiujishan on West Lake in Wulin.
The temple’s name was Zhengzhuan (Orthodox Transmission), and there exists a collection of verses titled "Ten Scenic Views of Zhengzhuan" within his works.
The Chan Master Daming Dufeng, whose name was Benshan, was a descendant of Fengyang.
Born while his father was serving in the region, he grew up in Leyang, Guangdong. His father’s surname was Wu.
Her mother was surnamed Zhong. From a young age, she treated Buddhist matters as a child’s play.

At seventeen, she left the household life and initially sought instruction from Master Yuanming, who showed her the "Mu" (No) kōan. In the eighth year of the Zhengtong era, she entered Min Province to study under Master Wujie;
upon hearing the sound of a bell, she attained realization. Subsequently, she visited Mengyin, then Chushan, and finally Yuexi, whose seal of approval she received.

He approved this. From the previous seven-day retreat (*qijiu*) in seclusion, he practiced without slackening day or night. Having exhausted a hundredfold of arduous effort, he attained great enlightenment (*daché*).

Subsequently, at the Mongol court, he was again invested with the robe and fly-whisk (*yifu*). In the *Gengchen* year of the Tian-shun era, Lady Zhao established the San-ta Temple on West Lake and invited the Master to be its founding abbot (*kaishan*).
He subsequently revived the Zhaoming Temple on Mount Tianmu, the Baolian Temple on Mount Wushan, and further revived...

Nanshan Amṛta. In the *Gengzi* year of the Chenghua era, he closed his retreat at Seokbuk-sa Temple. In the *Jinyin* year, there was a mountain called Dengyun on Jiyun-ryeong, where the temple named Cheonjin was located;

the monk Chonggang requested that the Master establish it there. Once the construction was completed, he immediately closed his retreat and withdrew from human affairs to cultivate and refine himself. He had a saying: "For over forty years, I have remained in strict seclusion. After his passing, his disciples... (Note:

The source text appears to be a fragment of a historical or biographical record concerning a Chinese Buddhist master’s life and activities in Korea, specifically mentioning dates, locations, and specific terminology such as *amṛta* [sweet dew] and the closing of a retreat.)
Renwu Shenjietxin and others compiled the Master’s discourses, deeds, and biography, titled *The Record of the Essential Words from the Three Locations:
Mingzhao, Mingganlu, and Tianzhen*. It states:
"The Chan Master Xueting [Ming] of the Great Ming."
The Master’s style name was Xueting; he was also known as the Recluse of Plum and Snow. His ancestral registration was in Renhe County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang Province.

His father’s surname was Gui and his given name was Zheng; his mother was of the Xu clan. There were three brothers, and the Master was the youngest. He was born in the Bingzi year of the Jingtai era.
Having lost his father at the age of seven and suffered from smallpox and wind-related ailments, he subsequently developed an eye disease. He repeatedly sought to leave the household life;

at fifteen, he searched for a teacher, yet found only that it increased his heterodox understandings. In the *guisi* year of the Chenghua era, he visited Master Xiuxiu at Xianlin Temple in the prefectural city.

Upon their first meeting, they reached a profound accord, and he was entrusted with the "No-Character" (*wuzi*) koan. At seventeen, he shaved his head and studied day and night, yet he remained stuck in a state of silent stagnation. He sat...

Formerly, Yuanmo urged me to study the teachings. While reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I encountered the passage about a jeweled royal land appearing upon the tip of a single hair and felt some doubt.
Later, while at Qianming Temple in Jiangyin, I suddenly beheld the golden and azure majesty of the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall towering before my eyes;

it was there that I unexpectedly realized the meaning of the phrase "a land appearing on the tip of a hair. On New Year’s Eve of the first year of the Hongzhi era, I heard the sound of the bells several times.
In his later years, his practice suddenly became vivid and liberated. He spoke these verses offhand: "The perfect resonance is not heard by the mind;
the great thousandfold world is a single illumination. Having brushed past the ultimate barrier, no further mysteries or subtleties remain.

In the year of Yi-mao (1235), he again followed Master Xiuxiu at Jingci Temple, whereupon he received formal certification (*inka*). Among his writings are the *Qingyi jingjin*, *Niangu songgu*, and *Yi Hanshan*.

Together with his *Yongming shiji* (Verses and Gāthās of Yongming) and other works, totaling twenty fascicles, these were titled the *Huanji ji* (Collection of Illusory Entrustment) and circulated in the world.
This concludes the *Xulu wulin xihu gaoseng shilüe* (Continued Brief Account of Eminent Monks of the West Lake in Wulin).
